planting.note: Root leaf or stem-tip cuttings in spring or summer in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; allow cut ends to callus for a day or two before inserting to avoid rot.

directions: Kalanchoe bracteata forms a multi-branched, woody-based shrublet with spoon-shaped leaves densely coated in silvery-white felt, giving the whole plant a frosted, metallic sheen rather than the coppery-bronze fuzz of the related Copper Spoons (K. orgyalis). New growth emerges nearly white and gradually shows more green as leaves mature and the felt thins with age. Grow in full sun with sharply draining soil, watering only after the mix has dried out completely, since the felted foliage holds moisture against the leaf surface and is prone to spotting if wetted overhead. Small clusters of pale flowers appear on upright stalks in winter, but the plant is grown almost entirely for its foliage color and texture rather than its bloom.

planting.note: Divide offsets or root short stem cuttings in spring in shallow, gritty succulent mix; the compact clumping habit makes division the faster route to new plants.

directions: This is a small, clump-forming kalanchoe that stays far more compact than the shrubby panda plant, with tight rosettes of grey-green leaves wrapped in a dense coat of fine white wool that gives the whole plant a snowy, felted appearance. Rosettes offset readily at the base to form a slow-spreading mat rather than a single upright stem, making it useful as a textural front-of-container or rock-garden accent among other small succulents. Grow in bright light with some protection from the hottest afternoon sun, in shallow, sharply draining mix, and water only once thoroughly dry, since the wool traps moisture and encourages rot if kept damp. Its miniature, groundcover-like scale distinguishes it clearly from the much larger tomentosa and beharensis already common in cultivation.

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets or take stem cuttings in spring, letting cut surfaces callus briefly before setting into well-drained succulent mix.

directions: Native to grassland habitats in South Africa, this clumping succulent forms low rosette clusters of glossy, scalloped-edged leaves that are green in shade but flush deep coppery-bronze to maroon under strong sun or cool temperatures, unlike the more powdery or velvet-textured foliage of fedtschenkoi and marnieriana. Short, dense spikes of tubular yellow flowers rise above the foliage in spring, giving it more floral interest than many foliage-grown kalanchoes. Grow in full sun in gritty, well-drained soil and allow the mix to dry between waterings; it tolerates light frost better than most tender kalanchoes but is still best treated as a container or greenhouse plant outside zones 9-11. Its glossy, non-fuzzy leaf surface and clumping rosette habit make it easy to distinguish from the felted or paddle-leaved kalanchoes already common in cultivation.
